readerTitle: The dream first customer who never paid
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소상공인 대상 배송 서비스, 기업 교육 컨설팅) · 실제 기업이나 수치는 쓰지 않음
insight: 디자인 파트너는 호의가 아니라 거래다. 서로 무엇을 주고받는지 약속이 있어야 학습도 매출도 남는다.
misconception: 크고 유명한 첫 고객이 무료로 함께 만들어 주겠다고 하면 무조건 기회다.

sources.text: 디자인 파트너(design partner)는 B2B 소프트웨어 창업에서 널리 쓰이는 일반적인 관행이며, 특정 연구나 기업 사례를 인용하지 않음

factChecks.note: 모든 사례와 설정(40개 매장 체인, 6개월 파일럿, 3곳의 독립 매장 등)은 가상입니다. 실제 통계나 연구 결과처럼 읽히는 문장이 없는지 게시 전 확인하세요.
'디자인 파트너'라는 용어가 엔터프라이즈 소프트웨어에서 흔히 쓰인다는 설명은 일반적 관행 서술입니다. 특정 기원이나 최초 사용자를 주장하지 않도록 문구를 유지하세요.
'3~5곳의 파트너'는 업계에서 흔히 쓰는 경험칙으로 제시했으며 연구 근거가 있는 수치가 아닙니다. 필요하면 'a handful'로 바꾸는 것을 검토하세요.

cards.title: The dream first customer who never paid
body: A founder starts a weekly restocking and delivery service for independent grocery shops. Before launch, a regional supermarket chain with 40 stores calls.
They offer a free six-month pilot. "Help us shape it," they say. It feels like the best possible start. It turns out to be the most expensive yes she says all year.

image.label: A small delivery van parked beside a giant supermarket
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 배송 밴이 거대한 슈퍼마켓 건물 앞에 서 있고, 건물 입구에 "Free pilot" 현수막. 멀리 작은 동네 가게 세 곳이 보임. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who should help shape your new service?
body: Your delivery service is built for small independent shops. The 40-store chain offers a free six-month pilot and sends a long list of requests.
Three independent shops are also interested, but they want a discount to try something new. What do you do?

options.text: Take the chain's free pilot. A big name will win over the small shops later
options.feedback: You gain a famous name, but you shape the service around a customer unlike your real market, with no promise they'll ever pay.

options.text: Sign the three shops at a discount, with monthly feedback calls and a set price after three months
options.feedback: Smaller names, but they match your target customer, and the deal itself tests whether they'll pay.

options.text: Take everyone and build whatever each of them asks for
options.feedback: More input, but the requests will pull in different directions. You risk a service that fits no one well.

cards.title: Six months of work, no contract.
body: She said yes to the chain and built what they asked for:
list: Stock reports in the chain's own format
Sunday deliveries for their busiest stores
Invoices that matched their buying system
cards.callout: At the end: "Great pilot. No budget this year." The small shops she met later needed none of those features. She had spent half a year building for a customer who was never going to buy.

cards.title: Design partners
body: A **design partner** is an early customer who helps shape what you're building. In return, they get early access, real influence and usually a better price.
The key word is *exchange*. A good partner gives time, honest feedback and a commitment, often to pay. A free pilot with no terms is a favor, and favors end politely.

image.label: Two-sided scale: what the founder gives and what the partner gives
image.brief: 양팔 저울 일러스트. 왼쪽 접시에 "Early access", "A say in the product", "Lower price". 오른쪽 접시에 "Time", "Honest feedback", "A decision to buy". 저울이 균형을 이룸. 로고 없음.

cards.title: What a real partner deal includes.
body: The terms matter more than the size of the partner.
list: **Fit:** they look like the customers you plan to sell to
**Several, not one:** a handful of partners, so no single voice steers everything
**Written give-and-get:** feedback sessions, access to their data, a fixed list of changes
**An end date and a decision:** will they buy, and at what price?
**Some payment:** even a small fee shows real need
cards.callout: If they won't commit to anything, they aren't a partner yet.
cards.softwareNote: Software startups often give partners early access and a discount in exchange for weekly calls and usage data. The classic trap is turning one partner's wish list into the whole product roadmap.

cards.title: The same deal works in any industry.
body: A bakery testing a wholesale line can sign two cafés that commit to weekly orders and honest notes on what sells. A cleaning company can design a new office service with three clients who agree to a review every month.
A parts maker can develop a new component with one buyer who agrees to a first order if the samples pass. Each time, both sides know what they give, what they get and when the decision comes.

cards.title: Partners are early, not typical.
body: Design partners are keener and more patient than most customers. What delights them may not sell to everyone else, so check their requests against the wider market.

Discounts can stick. The first price you give often becomes the price a customer expects to keep paying. And agree early on who owns what you build together, especially when a partner shares data or designs.

cards.title: Now it's a training firm.
body: You run a consulting firm launching a new staff onboarding program for mid-size companies. A large bank wants to be your first client.
They ask you to rebuild the program around their own HR system and run it free, "since we're helping you." What do you offer?

options.text: Agree to their terms. A bank as a client will open doors
options.feedback: You get a strong reference, but you spend months on one bank's setup with no payment and no promise to buy.

options.text: Offer partner terms: reduced fee, a fixed list of changes, monthly feedback, a buying decision by month four. Recruit two mid-size firms too
options.feedback: You keep the bank's input but on clear terms, and the mid-size firms keep the program shaped for your real market.

options.text: Decline and sell only the finished program at full price
options.feedback: You protect your price and focus, but you lose the early input a rough new program needs most.

cards.title: A design partner is a deal, not a favor.
body: Pick partners who look like your market, take more than one, and write down what each side gives and when the decision comes.
**Try it today:** list three things you'd ask an early customer to give you, and three things you'd give back.
